platforms.title: 3 Signs That Separate a Yeast Infection From BV
platforms.meta_description: Unusual discharge with an odd smell? How the ACOG tells a yeast infection apart from bacterial vaginosis, by discharge texture, smell, and itching.
platforms.body_html:
Discharge that looks different than usual, with a smell that's throwing you off, and reaching for an antifungal cream from the pharmacy without knowing for sure? The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) explains that a yeast infection and bacterial vaginosis (BV) come from completely different microorganisms. The symptoms can overlap, but the treatments are entirely different, so using the wrong one means it won't clear up and tends to come right back.

Why they look similar but come from different causes

A yeast infection is an overgrowth of a fungus called Candida. It's marked by thick, white, clumpy discharge with a cottage-cheese texture, usually with no odor, along with intense itching and burning. It commonly shows up after taking antibiotics, with high blood sugar, or from wearing tight clothing often.

Bacterial vaginosis comes from an entirely different microorganism. It's marked by a drop in the lactobacteria that normally protect the vagina, allowing other anaerobic bacteria to overgrow, producing thin, grayish-white discharge with a fishy odor. Itching is usually mild or absent, and the smell often gets noticeably worse after sex or washing.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, the texture and smell of the discharge. The ACOG notes this is the single most reliable way to distinguish them. Thick, clumpy, and odorless leans toward a yeast infection, while thin, grayish, and fishy-smelling leans toward BV.

Second, whether the itching is intense, or the smell is the more noticeable problem. A yeast infection brings clear itching and burning, while BV's main discomfort tends to be the odor rather than itching.

What matters most is not repeatedly buying antifungal cream from the pharmacy without knowing which one it actually is. Using an antifungal on BV does nothing at all, since BV needs a prescription antibiotic instead. Leaving BV untreated raises the risk of picking up a sexually transmitted infection, and during pregnancy it can raise the risk of complications like preterm labor, so it's not something to brush off lightly.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to note the color and texture of the discharge, whether there's an odor, how intense the itching is, and whether there's been recent sex or douching, or recent antibiotic use. If symptoms keep recurring or it's still unclear, getting an accurate diagnosis with a vaginal swab test at an OB-GYN is the safest move.

The risk factors point in different directions too. Yeast infections tend to follow antibiotic use, uncontrolled blood sugar, or tight, damp clothing that traps moisture. BV tends to follow having a new or multiple sexual partners, not using condoms, or douching, which strips away the protective bacteria the vagina relies on rather than cleaning anything useful away.

If the same symptoms keep coming back again and again despite treatment, that's worth mentioning specifically at the appointment, since recurring cases sometimes call for a longer treatment course or a closer look at what keeps triggering the imbalance in the first place, rather than just repeating the same short course each time.

Is your discharge right now thick and clumpy with itching, or thin with a fishy smell?
